Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?

summaries.gardner: Accenture is a dominant, well-run leader with strong management, but it lacks most Rule Breaker traits: its industry is mature and growing mid-single digits, it is not a consumer-recognized top dog, and the stock has lagged badly rather than shown strong momentum. It fits a Rule Maker profile better than a Rule Breaker one.
summaries.buffett: Accenture has an understandable business, a consistent record (revenue up every year since FY2021 to $74.2B), low debt, high returns on capital (about 28% ROIC) and strong free cash flow of $11.6B. Its moat is moderate rather than wide because the work is people-based and competitive, but at about 17x trailing earnings after a large share-price fall it is closer to a fair price for a good business than it has been in years.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the high returns on capital, conservative balance sheet and simple business, and would focus on the main way it could fail: AI shrinking the billable hours its model depends on. The question is whether Accenture's scale and client relationships let it capture AI work faster than it loses traditional work.
summaries.lynch: Accenture is a stalwart: a large, steady grower (revenue +6.5% in FY2026, adjusted EPS +8%) that has shrunk its diluted share count from 646M to 605M. With a P/E of about 17 against mid-to-high single-digit earnings growth, the PEG is well above 1, so it is not a Lynch bargain, though it is now unloved after a 38% five-year total-return decline.
summaries.fisher: Accenture scores well on sales ability, management depth and investing in new capabilities ($1B R&D and $1B training in FY2026, nearly 110,000 AI and data specialists). It scores less well on profit-margin improvement, since operating margins have stayed around 15% for years.
summaries.graham: Accenture passes Graham's size, financial-strength, ten-year profitability, dividend-record and earnings-growth tests, but fails the price tests: the P/E on three-year average earnings is about 18.5 and P/E times P/B is about 73, far above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Accenture is a services company in a crowded, competitive market rather than a monopoly with proprietary technology, so it does poorly on Thiel's questions about 10x technology and unique secrets. Its strengths are distribution (sales relationships with most large enterprises) and durability so far.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner focuses on AI platform shifts, growth plus margin discipline and valuation; Accenture is positioned as an AI implementer but is growing only mid-single digits and is seen by many investors as a potential AI loser. At about 16x forward earnings and an 8.6% free-cash-flow yield the price is undemanding, so the debate centres on whether AI helps or hurts its revenue.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and catalysts; Accenture's growth is steady but not accelerating (FY2027 guide 3%-6% local currency), though a sharp rally from the June 2026 low after a Q4 beat shows sentiment can turn. It is unlikely to be a high-conviction concentrated position on his terms.
summaries.smith: Accenture fits much of Terry Smith's 'good company' test: high return on capital, little debt, strong cash conversion and a long record, though its 32% gross margin is lower than he typically prefers. At today's price it is far from overpaid relative to its history.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Accenture combines a high return on capital (about 28% ROIC) with an earnings yield of about 8.6% (FY2026 operating income of $11.4B against an enterprise value of about $133B), a reasonably attractive combination for a large company.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs are a great business, skilled and honest management, and reinvestment opportunities; Accenture has the first two to a fair degree, and reinvests through roughly $5B a year of acquisitions while also returning about $11.5B to shareholders, so reinvestment at high returns is only partly available.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for low-risk, high-uncertainty bets in simple businesses; Accenture is simple, has net cash and strong free cash flow, and has been sold off on AI fears, so the downside looks limited. However the discount is moderate rather than the deep bargain he usually seeks.
summaries.wood: Accenture is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense: it sells services that help others adopt AI rather than building an innovation platform with falling unit costs. It would not fit ARK's focus areas.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry at reasonable prices; Accenture is predictable and cash-rich with low leverage, but its barriers to entry are only moderate and growth has slowed.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economies-shared businesses; Accenture shares some of its scale with clients through investment in AI tools and training, but it does not systematically lower prices as it grows, and its position in 10-20 years depends on adapting to AI.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge new markets with great technology; Accenture is a mature, 30-plus-year-old services firm, so it does not fit a venture framework.
summaries.nash: Accenture fails several of Tom Nash's hard filters, including revenue growth below 10%, an operating margin below 20% and a five-year return far behind the S&P 500, and scores about 70 on his 13-category scale. Its balance sheet, free cash flow and valuation (a DCF value of about $251 per share at a 12% discount rate) are strengths.

momentum.evidence: At $229.68 (Oct 16, 2026) the stock is down about 4% over 52 weeks per StockAnalysis while the S&P 500 rose, despite a sharp rebound from a June 2026 low of $118.15.

g4.evidence: Julie Sweet is a widely respected CEO (TIME100, WSJ best-managed company recognition) and Accenture partners with Microsoft, AWS, Google, Nvidia and Anthropic, but it is not backed by a famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: After falling about 57% from its peak to the June 2026 low, commentators generally call Accenture cheap or an AI loser rather than overvalued; the forward P/E is about 15.7.

simple.evidence: Accenture sells consulting and managed IT services by the hour or by contract to large organizations, a model a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Accenture has been profitable every year in the last decade, revenue rose every year from $50.5B in FY2021 to $74.2B in FY2026, and diluted EPS rose from $6.45 in FY2016 to $13.56 in FY2026.

integrity.evidence: Management reports bookings and guidance consistently, returned a record $11.5B to shareholders in FY2026, carries modest debt (less than cash) and has had no accounting controversies, though the CEO also serves as chair.

b6.evidence: Accenture is a serial acquirer ($4.9B on 17 deals in FY2026, about $5B planned in FY2027), but deals are mostly small tuck-ins aimed at new capabilities rather than empire-building.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 28% and return on equity about 26% (StockAnalysis), with debt of $10.1B below cash of $12.8B.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $11.62B against net income of $8.52B, a conversion above 100%.

b10.evidence: Over the last five years Accenture retained and reinvested billions, yet its five-year total return was negative 38% (Trefis, Sept 2026), so market value did not keep pace.

safety.evidence: A Nash-style DCF at a 12% discount rate gives about $251 per share, roughly 9% above the $229.68 price, a modest margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: At about 17x trailing GAAP EPS of $13.56, 15.7x forward estimates and an 8.6% free-cash-flow yield, the price is reasonable for a high-return, steady-growth business.

mu5.evidence: Accenture has net cash, diverse clients and industries, but AI automation that shrinks labor-based billing is a credible way the business could erode.

reinvest.evidence: It reinvests about $5B a year in acquisitions plus $1B each in R&D and training, but most free cash flow is returned to shareholders because high-return reinvestment opportunities are limited.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart: a large company growing revenue mid-single digits and EPS high-single digits with buybacks and a rising dividend.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 17 is well above expected EPS growth of about 5%-9% (FY2027 GAAP EPS guide +6% to +9%).

runway.evidence: AI, data centers, cybersecurity and sovereign AI give new avenues, but consensus expects only about 4%-5% revenue growth in FY2027.

ly7.evidence: Insiders hold only about 0.04% and are not open-market buyers, but the diluted share count fell from 645.9M in FY2021 to 605.3M in Q4 FY2026.

ly8.evidence: Accenture is covered by 27 analysts and is a widely held large cap, though currently out of favour.

fi2.evidence: Management keeps building new offerings, from advanced AI (400+ clients started advanced AI work in FY2026) to OT cybersecurity via Dragos.

fi3.evidence: Its $1B R&D spend supports AI tools and assets, but the payoff is hard to measure and revenue growth has stayed mid-single digits.

fi4.evidence: FY2026 new bookings were $84.5B with a record 141 quarterly client bookings above $100M, evidence of an unusually strong sales engine.

longterm.evidence: Accenture invests heavily in training and AI capabilities and keeps acquiring, but it also manages tightly to quarterly margin and EPS targets.

gr1.evidence: FY2026 revenue was $74.2B and market value is about $136B.

ni10.evidence: Accenture has reported positive net income every year from FY2016 ($4.35B) through FY2026 ($8.52B).

gr4.evidence: Accenture has paid a cash dividend every year since at least November 2005, about 21 years, and declared $1.71 per quarter in October 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $6.45 in FY2016 to $13.56 in FY2026, more than doubling.

gr6.evidence: At $229.68 the price is about 18.5 times average diluted EPS of the last three years ($11.44, $12.15, $13.56).

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 16.9 times price/book of about 4.3 gives roughly 73, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Accenture sells services, not proprietary technology that is ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Enterprise AI adoption creates demand for implementation work, but clients are moving slowly and AI also threatens labor-based revenue, as the 2026 sell-off showed.

th3.evidence: Accenture is already the largest firm in a large, fragmented market, not a company dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Accenture's management is highly regarded and executes consistently, but it is not led by an exceptional founder.

th5.evidence: Its distribution is a key strength: relationships with 317 Diamond clients and most of the world's largest companies.

durable.evidence: Its client relationships and scale have lasted decades, but AI could shrink or reshape the labor-based IT-services model within 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Accenture competes in a well-understood market against many large rivals rather than a unique opportunity others miss.

trend.evidence: It is a major AI and cloud implementation partner (nearly 110,000 AI and data professionals), but many investors see it as a potential loser from AI automation.

dr1.evidence: Growth is steady rather than accelerating: FY2026 revenue +6.5% and FY2027 guidance of 3%-6% local currency, with consensus FY2027 EPS growth about 5%.

dr2.evidence: Results in 18-24 months depend on whether AI work offsets pricing pressure; there is no clear evidence yet either way.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates and a stronger economy would help discretionary consulting demand, and a weaker dollar boosted FY2026 USD growth, but a hawkish Fed weighed on IT stocks in mid-2026.

dr6.evidence: Possible catalysts include the Dragos OT-cyber acquisition, recovery in federal work and AI bookings growth, but none is transformative.

dr7.evidence: With mid-single-digit growth and real AI disruption risk, conviction is unlikely to be high enough for a concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin (revenue less cost of services) was about 32% in FY2026, typical for IT services and low compared with software.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow of $11.62B against a market value of about $135.7B is an 8.6% yield, attractive for a high-ROIC business.

gb2.evidence: FY2026 operating income of $11.41B against an enterprise value of about $133B is roughly an 8.6% earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The share-price fall reflects fears about AI and weak discretionary spending; the spending slump looks temporary, but the AI threat may be structural.

pa4.evidence: With cash exceeding debt, $11.6B of annual free cash flow and diversified clients, permanent loss of capital looks unlikely at this valuation.

wo1.evidence: Accenture is an AI services provider, not a leader in building AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing platforms.

wo2.evidence: As a people-based services firm, its costs do not fall quickly with volume.

wo3.evidence: It implements other firms' innovation platforms rather than combining its own.

wo4.evidence: Consensus expects only about 4%-7% annual revenue growth, not a multiple-fold expansion of its market in five years.

ac3.evidence: It is insulated from commodity prices and has little debt, but demand for consulting is sensitive to the economy and FX moves its reported revenue.

ns1.evidence: Accenture shares scale benefits through AI tools and productivity gains passed to clients at renewal, but it does not deliberately cut prices as it grows.

ns4.evidence: Whether its position will be stronger in 10-20 years depends on AI's effect on services demand, which is unclear.

va2.evidence: It helps large organizations modernize complex technology and operations, a large and costly problem for them.

tn1.evidence: Accenture sells into AI and cloud adoption, but it is an established services business adapting to the trend rather than one built for it.

tn2.evidence: The market treats Accenture as an AI loser, while it is pushing into AI, data centers and OT cybersecurity; whether that gap is real is unproven.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap, non-Chinese, non-commodity, non-seasonal and long-established company.

tn4.evidence: It passes all three: revenue grew every year since FY2021, FY2026 net income was $8.52B, and cash of $12.84B exceeded debt of $10.11B.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive in recent quarters (Q4 FY2026 $2.85B, Q3 $3.60B), and cash exceeded debt at each recent quarter-end, including $12.84B vs $10.11B at Aug 31, 2026.

tn6.evidence: FY2026 revenue grew 6.5% in USD and 5% in local currency; FY2027 guidance is 3%-6%.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 6.5% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 15.7% gives about 22, below 40.

tn8.evidence: FY2026 revenue rose 6.5% while total operating expenses rose 5.6% ($62.78B vs $59.45B).

tn9.evidence: It trips instant kills: operating margin of 15.4% is below 20%, and revenue growth below 10% fell from 7.4% in FY2025 to 6.5% in FY2026.

tn10.evidence: There is no major legal threat, but US federal spending cuts and data and AI regulation pose moderate risks.

tn11.evidence: Accenture provides consulting and technology services that help large organizations modernize and run their operations, charging fees for projects and multi-year managed-services contracts; clients choose it for scale and breadth.

tn13.evidence: Total about 70/100: cash vs debt 5, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10 (3.3%), institutional ownership 10 (85%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year and cash exceeded debt every year, but operating margin did not expand (15.2% FY2022, 13.7% FY2023, 15.4% FY2026) and free cash flow dipped in FY2024 ($8.61B from $9.00B).

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 38x, current ratio 1.43 and liabilities 1.2x equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($46.8B) are only 1.16x liabilities ($40.3B), below 2x.

tn18.evidence: Julie Sweet has a solid execution record since 2019, but she has been CEO only about seven years, is not a founder and has not made open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Accenture beat EPS consensus in Q3 FY2026 ($3.80 vs $3.69) and beat Q4 FY2026 revenue consensus ($18.68B vs $18.04B), but Q3 revenue was slightly short of estimates.

tn21.evidence: No fraud, auditor change (KPMG) or co-CEO structure, but it is a heavy acquirer (17 deals in FY2026) and the CEO is a regular seller, not a buyer.

tn22.evidence: It has $74.2B of revenue, strong profits and buys back shares rather than issuing them.

tn24.evidence: At a 10% discount rate and its 14.8% average FCF margin, the $229.68 price implies revenue shrinking roughly 4% a year, below the 6.5% growth it delivered in FY2026.

tn25.evidence: Using 3-year averages (revenue growth about 5.0%, FCF margin about 14.8%), 4% terminal growth, a 12% discount rate and net cash of about $2.7B, value comes out near $251 per share, above $229.68.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 15.7 is below IBM's but above Cognizant and Capgemini, and with expected EPS growth around 5%-8% the PEG is about 2, above 1.
